Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Burlington VT
713 AM EDT Sun Sep 20 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 249 AM EDT Sunday...

No significant changes made with this forecast package.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 249 AM EDT Sunday...

1. Light rain and cool temperatures today, then a prolonged dry 
and seasonably cool weather stretch begins.   

2. Dry weather persists through mid week, though we will need 
to monitor for increasing shower chances from Friday onward.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 249 AM EDT Sunday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: A widespread light rainfall event remains on track for 
today. There has been a slight trend towards less rainfall and 
shorter duration of rain, as well as lower chances for rain in the 
St. Lawrence Valley. That being said, the forecast generally is 
pretty consistent with observations so far early this morning. 
Moisture advection from the south and southwest, particularly from 
the surface up to 700 millibars, is occurring with a sharp gradient, 
while westerly mid-level/upper level is present. An inverted trough 
in northern New York and weak surface low sliding eastward across 
northern Pennsylvania will support modest southeasterly winds across 
the Champlain Valley and points east. 

Stratiform rain will blossom in northern New York and gradually
expand east-northeastward this morning. During the afternoon, 
the area of rain will contract from west to east and towards the
southeast as the 850 millibar trough axis and associated low 
level convergence and lift exits. Rainfall rates will be 0.01 - 
0.05" for most of the event, but up to a few hours intensity 
will likely increase and reach the 0.1"-0.15" range (typically 
considered "moderate" rather than light). These moderate 
rainfall rates are favored from the Adirondacks eastward over 
most of northern Vermont at times from about 10 AM and 3 PM. As 
a result, event totals, as they would be for a winter weather 
event, are somewhat uncertain but should be mostly in the 0.25" 
to 0.5" range within much of the region. 

Temperatures today will generally be chilly in the low to mid 50s 
with thick clouds and rain for much of the day, and even cooler in 
portions of central/eastern Vermont due to the aforementioned 
upslope easterly component to the wind. It is a tricky hourly 
temperature forecast with large dependence on rainfall timing; 
as a result, there is potential for late day highs where rain 
ends early enough and morning highs in northern and eastern 
portions of Vermont prior to rain arriving.
 
Tonight we'll lock in some low clouds and patchy fog ahead of a
moisture starved cold front arriving from the northwest. Once 
this boundary passes through, northerly flow will develop with
some low clouds slow to clear out, especially in the vicinity 
of the higher terrain with moist 925-850 millibar air expected
to linger into the day. Clouds should gradually scatter
generally from north to south, leading to the beginning of a
prolonged stretch of primarily clear skies. Fog chances in climo
favored areas will begin high Tuesday, but tend to decrease 
each morning following days of drying after Sunday's rainfall.
Temperatures will remain below normal through Wednesday with the
dominance of strong high pressure to our north supplying us 
with seasonably cool air.

KEY MESSAGE 2: The blocking pattern will remain in place much of next 
week, with high pressure centered to our north while low pressure 
develops off the Mid Atlantic. While our weather will be pleasant, 
temperatures will likely remain below normal, with daytime highs 
mainly in the 60s. Clear skies and light winds will allow for chilly 
overnights, and patchy frost will be possible in the 
Adirondacks/eastern VT valleys each morning. While confidence has 
increased in the dry weather persisting through Thursday, low 
pressure meandering around off the East Coast will keep the threat 
of showers around as we head toward the weekend, especially in 
southern/eastern VT. Have stayed with the NBM/WPC forecast for 
Friday onward given the spread in model solutions for mid/late next 
week.

&&

.AVIATION /12Z SUNDAY THROUGH THURSDAY/...
Through 12Z Monday...Deteriorating conditions expected this
morning as rain spreads over the region. Ceilings will lower to
1500-2500 ft by 16z at all terminals. Upstream observations and
model guidance indicates the potential for IFR ceilings, but
confidence in this remains somewhat low. The exception is at
SLK, where ceilings should drop below 1000 ft for several hours
this afternoon/evening. Visibility generally 4-6SM in rain,
which will exit to the east by 00z Mon. Ceilings may improve for
a bit thereafter, but widespread MVFR/local IFR develop after
06z with a cold frontal passage, particularly in northern areas
and in the higher terrain. S/SW winds less than 10 kt through
the daylight hours, becoming near calm with sunset. Winds start
to shift to the N/NW late in the TAF period with the cold
frontal passage. 

Outlook...

Monday: Mainly VFR, with local IFR possible. NO SIG WX.
Monday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Tuesday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Tuesday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Wednesday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Wednesday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Thursday: VFR. NO SIG WX.

&&

.MARINE...
As of 249 AM EDT Sunday...

Expect south-southeast winds this morning to ramp up but remain
below Lake Wind Advisory criteria, peaking around 9 AM just 
above 20 knots in the vicinity of Colchester Reef before 
settling into the 15-20 knot range during the rest of the day. 
Waves should build up to 3 feet.

Following a lull in winds tonight, a favorable setup for well
mixed northerly winds will develop for Monday when a Lake Wind
Advisory may be needed. Waves could build up to 3 to 4 feet over
the southern waters during the Monday morning period associated
with these gusty north winds.

&&

.BTV WATCHES/WARNINGS/ADVISORIES...
VT...None.
NY...None.

&&
